newsitem.title: USA: IMF said to delay Russian loan tranche.
newsitem.headline: IMF said to delay Russian loan tranche.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund was still not happy with Russia's revenue collections and planned to hold up another disbursement of its three-year $10 billion loan to Russia, retiring U.S. Ambassador to Moscow Thomas Pickering said on Thursday.
But he told the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace that Moscow was very serious about meeting the IMF targets and would make a major effort this month to do that.

"I'm disappointed that an IMF mission which just finished an early examination -- the real major examination will come at the end of this month -- is still not satisfied with the level of revenue collection," said Pickering, who just completed a three-and-a-half-year tour in Moscow.

"So the revenue collection target has defeated the capacity -- at least for the moment -- for the IMF to disburse another important tranche in the long-term stabilisation fund loan on which Russia is counting," he said.

He called this "agonizing" for Russia's economy and added that the dangers of Russia not getting the IMF loan "are real in the sense that social dislocation for many people in Russia are just around the corner."
The IMF has already delayed handing over one tranche of its three-year $10 billion loan to Russia because it was worried about low tax revenues.
On Wednesday, Russian central bank head Sergei Dubinin told Reuters Financial Television in Paris: "Our chances to receive the new tranche are better in November than October."
Dubinin said the IMF was helping Russia solve what he described as a key problem and declined to confirm that negotiations with the IMF were particularly difficult.
Earlier he told a bankers' conference he was convinced tax collection targets would be met.
"We hope that the monthly examination in November will be passed and we will be able to met these objectives, and therefore the (IMF) tranches will be paid in time," he said.

Moscow would make a major effort in the months ahead to improve tax collection, through administrative and police action if necessary. "We are going to adopt much stricter rules on tax collection," he said.
In Moscow on Thursday, a top minister said Russia may have to run the risk of displeasing its international creditors in order to pay millions of dollars in overdue pensions.

"The situation with debts for pensions is so serious that it seems we may have to go ahead with a decision that might not please certain international monetary organisations," First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin told the Federation Council upper house of parliament.
IMF representatives arrive in Moscow on Thursday for talks on paying out the latest delayed tranche of the $10 billion loan.
